previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old female was admitted with right ankle pain, erythema, and increased swelling, diagnosed as right lower extremity cellulitis. She had a history of recurrent cellulitis, morbid obesity, and chronic anasarca. IV vancomycin was started, and a PICC line was placed for continued outpatient antibiotic therapy. Ultrasounds ruled out DVT in both the right leg and arm, with the latter showing IV infiltration. Her INR was subtherapeutic at 1.1, prompting an increase in warfarin and temporary heparin prophylaxis. She was diuresed with IV Lasix, and her oral diuretic regimen was intensified at discharge. She refused rehab and was discharged home with visiting nurse services for IV antibiotics, INR monitoring, and lab follow-up.

Impression: Patient is a ___ y/o F with PMHx significant for 
morbid obesity, recurrent cellulitis, who presents for shortness 
of breath and ___ swelling thought to have recurrence of 
cellulitis. We also noted significant ___ edema and volume 
overload concerning for diastolic dysfunction which improved 
with diuretics. We noted improvement in her leg symptoms with a 
combination of diuretics and IV antibiotics, and recommended 
close follow-up to ensure resolution of her symptoms. 
  
#Cellulitis- Initially antibiotics were held as ___ changes were 
thought to be ___ venous stasis changes. However, given patient 
has a good sense of her clinical situation, and she believes 
these are cellulitic changes, we will initiate antibiotics. 
Additionally, she does have recurrent cellulitis treated with 
Vancomycin and s/p skin flap, and therefore, at risk for 
compilcations should this not be treated adequately.  PICC line 
was placed and she was initiated on IV Vancomycin at 1500 mg q 
12 hrs.  She was also diuresed with PO torsemide as she did not 
have an IV at the time.  She was discharged with IV vancomycin 
for a ___s well as PO torsemide, to which she 
responded well during the admission.

#Shortness of Breath- patient had one episode of transient 
shortness of breath the night before admission, and was noted to 
have rales bilaterally in her lungs on admission which improved 
with diuresis. We did not note a recent echo in our system.  
This was likely due to fluid overload as she was diuresed, and 
potentially diastolic dysfunction, and symptoms had largely 
resolved, although we did feel that she would benefit from 
ongoing diuretic use and recommended ongoing therapy with 
diuretics.  PE was less likely given supratherapeutic INR. We 
did recommend that she proceed with a surface echo if one had 
not been obtained in the recent past, to clarify her pulmonary 
pressures and EF, and guide further medication management of her 
___ edema. She was discharged with home services with the hope of 
close blood work monitoring with results to be sent to her 
internist.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  History of bilateral swelling of lower extremities.

___ and ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Grayscale, color, and spectral Doppler evaluation was performed on
the bilateral lower extremity veins.

FINDINGS:  There is normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation of the
bilateral common femoral, proximal femoral, mid femoral, distal femoral and
popliteal veins.  Normal color flow and compressibility are demonstrated in
the posterior tibial and peroneal veins bilaterally.  There is normal
respiratory variation in the common femoral veins bilaterally. Note is made of
bilateral lower extremity soft tissue edema, left greater than right.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of a DVT in either lower extremity.

HISTORY:  ___ female with dyspnea on exertion.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:

Frontal and lateral views of the chest.  Previously seen left PICC is no
longer visualized.  The lungs are clear without effusion, consolidation or
pulmonary vascular congestion.  Cardiomediastinal silhouette is within normal
limits.  No acute osseous abnormality detected.

IMPRESSION:

No acute cardiopulmonary process.

HISTORY:  PICC placement.

FINDINGS:  Frontal and oblique views show the tip of the PICC line at about
the level of the aortic arch in the upper portion of the SVC.  In discussion
with the resident, the line will be pushed forward at least 6 cm if possible.

INDICATIONS:  Evaluate PICC placement.

COMPARISONS:  Chest radiographs from earlier on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  A single upright oblique view of the chest was obtained.

FINDINGS:  Again, the PICC tip is at the level of the aortic arch, likely in
the very upper SVC.  This is in high position, and could be advanced.  The
lungs are otherwise clear, though the exam is limited by patient positioning.

IMPRESSION:  PICC tip in the very high SVC.  Consider advancing for a more
secure position within the SVC.
